questions.stem: The Balance of Payments (BoP) of a country records all economic transactions between residents of the country and the rest of the world over a specified period. The two principal accounts of the BoP are:

options.option_text: Revenue Account and Capital Account
Current Account and Capital Account
Fiscal Account and Monetary Account
Trade Account and Invisibles Account

questions.explanation: Balance of Payments has TWO principal accounts: (1) CURRENT ACCOUNT — records trade in goods and services plus primary income (investment income, compensation of employees) and secondary income (current transfers, remittances); (2) CAPITAL ACCOUNT / FINANCIAL ACCOUNT — records transactions in financial assets/liabilities (FDI, FPI, loans, reserves). Option D is close but 'Trade Account' (goods only) and 'Invisibles Account' are SUB-PARTS of the Current Account, not the principal accounts themselves. 'Revenue Account' (option A) is a budget/government-accounting term, not BoP. Option C conflates fiscal vs monetary policy — different concept entirely.

questions.stem: In India's Balance of Payments accounting, which of the following is recorded under the CURRENT ACCOUNT (not the Capital Account)?

options.option_text: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflow
Remittances sent by an NRI in the USA to family in India
External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) taken by an Indian company
Sale of a real-estate property abroad by an Indian resident

questions.explanation: Remittances (private transfers) are classified under the Current Account's SECONDARY INCOME (also called Current Transfers) sub-heading — they don't create any claim or liability, so they aren't capital-account items. FDI (option A) creates an ownership stake → capital account. ECB (option C) creates a debt liability → capital account. Sale of overseas real estate (option D) is a disposal of an asset → capital account. India is historically the world's largest recipient of remittances (~USD 125 billion in recent years from migrant workers in Gulf, USA, UK) — a crucial BoP cushion.

questions.stem: India's MERCHANDISE TRADE DEFICIT (goods imports > goods exports) is persistently financed by which category of Current-Account INFLOWS?

options.option_text: FDI inflows only
Net INVISIBLES
RBI's sale of government securities to foreign buyers
Sovereign gold bonds floated domestically

questions.explanation: India structurally runs a MERCHANDISE (goods) trade deficit — roughly USD 250 bn/year in recent years, driven by crude-oil imports. The deficit is LARGELY financed by strong NET INVISIBLES EARNINGS (services + remittances): (i) IT/BPM services exports (~USD 200 bn/year); (ii) remittances (~USD 125 bn); (iii) tourism. Combined, these offset most of the goods deficit and keep the overall Current Account Deficit (CAD) manageable (~1-2 % of GDP in normal years). FDI (option A) is Capital Account, not Current. Option C is a Capital Account transaction. Option D is a domestic instrument — not a BoP item. primarily remittances, software services exports, and tourism earnings.

_fixes.was: Net INVISIBLES — primarily remittances, software services exports, and tourism earnings
_fixes.moved_to_explanation: primarily remittances, software services exports, and tourism earnings

questions.stem: If India's Current Account Deficit (CAD) + Capital Account Surplus = positive overall balance, the RBI typically responds by:

options.option_text: Selling foreign exchange reserves to tighten forex supply
Buying foreign exchange from the market, ADDING to its forex reserves
Printing INR to match the dollar inflow
Mandating all Indian exporters to convert to INR immediately

questions.explanation: BoP identity: Current Account + Capital Account = 0 (when you include the official reserve transactions). If CAD (−) is MORE THAN OFFSET by Capital Account Surplus (+), there's a net dollar inflow into the economy. To prevent excessive INR appreciation, RBI INTERVENES by BUYING the excess USD from the market, accumulating forex reserves. The reverse happens when CAD exceeds inflows — RBI sells reserves to protect the INR. India's forex reserves crossed USD 650 bn in 2024, among the world's largest. Option A is the opposite response. Option C describes naive monetary expansion — RBI sterilises such INR creation via OMOs. Option D is not a policy tool.

questions.stem: Which of the following transactions would IMPROVE (increase the surplus / reduce the deficit of) India's CURRENT account?

options.option_text: An Indian auto company imports machinery from Germany
An Indian software firm exports services to a US client
Foreign investors buy Indian government bonds
The government takes a loan from the IMF

questions.explanation: Services exports = Current Account CREDIT (inflow of foreign exchange for services rendered) → improves CAD. Option A is a merchandise import → Current Account DEBIT → WORSENS the deficit. Options C and D are CAPITAL Account transactions (bond purchases and loans create liabilities) → don't directly affect the Current Account (though they finance it). The Current Account cares about 'real' flows — goods, services, income, transfers. Capital Account cares about changes in asset positions.

questions.stem:
Match each BoP sub-component with the correct principal account and pick the correct pairing:
(i) Merchandise trade — Current Account
(ii) Software services exports — Current Account
(iii) Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) — Capital Account
(iv) NRI remittances — Current Account

options.option_text: Only (i) and (ii) correctly paired
Only (i), (ii), (iii) correctly paired
All four (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) correctly paired
Only (iii) correctly paired

questions.explanation: ALL four pairings are correct. CURRENT Account: merchandise trade (goods), services (incl. software exports), primary income (compensation, investment income), secondary income (remittances, grants). CAPITAL Account (or Financial Account in IMF terminology): FDI, FPI, External Commercial Borrowings, loans, banking capital, changes in reserves. Memorising 'which side of the BoP does X go on' is the #1 drill for Economics GK in Bank exams. Classic confusion: remittances feel like money transfer (capital-ish), but they're UNREQUITED transfers with no asset-liability creation, so Current Account.

questions.stem: The term 'TWIN DEFICIT' — a recurring concern in Indian macroeconomic discussions — refers to simultaneous:

options.option_text: Fiscal deficit (Revenue + Capital expenditure > Revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) AND Current Account Deficit
Current Account Deficit AND Capital Account Deficit
Trade Deficit AND Invisibles Deficit
Primary Deficit AND Revenue Deficit

questions.explanation: TWIN DEFICIT = FISCAL DEFICIT + CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT occurring together. The concern: a government running a fiscal deficit borrows → if borrowing is large and savings are low, the economy has to attract foreign capital → pressures INR → can push the CAD up. Worst case: a 'spiral' where both deficits self-reinforce. Notable Indian episodes: 1991 BoP crisis, 2013 'taper tantrum' crisis. Option B is rare/impossible structurally — a CAD is typically FINANCED by a Capital Account Surplus, so they're usually opposite signs. Options C and D describe other fiscal-terminology deficits.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In the IMF's BoP Manual (BPM6) — which India follows — the CAPITAL ACCOUNT and the FINANCIAL ACCOUNT are treated as:

options.option_text: Completely identical terms used interchangeably

Distinct — 'Capital Account' covers capital transfers (e.g. debt forgiveness) and non-produced non-financial assets; 'Financial Account' covers financial asset/liability transactions (FDI, FPI, loans, reserves)
'Capital Account' was renamed to 'Current Transfer Account' in BPM6
'Financial Account' refers to purely domestic banking

questions.explanation: Under IMF BPM6 (used by the RBI): CAPITAL ACCOUNT is narrow — it covers (a) capital transfers like debt forgiveness, migrants' transfers, government-to-government grants; (b) non-produced non-financial assets (e.g. patents sold to a foreign party). FINANCIAL ACCOUNT is much larger — FDI, FPI, External Debt, Banking Capital, Rupee Debt Service, Other Capital, and changes in RBI Reserves. Many Indian textbooks (pre-BPM6) used 'Capital Account' loosely to mean what is now 'Financial Account' — this is a common exam trap. RBI's monthly BoP release uses the modern BPM6 definitions.

questions.stem: The 1991 BALANCE OF PAYMENTS CRISIS in India was famously resolved after the government pledged GOLD to secure a short-term loan from which international authority?

options.option_text: The World Bank
The Bank of England (and later the Bank of Japan) against a physical gold pledge
The Asian Development Bank
The Federal Reserve Bank of the United States

questions.explanation: In 1991, India's forex reserves had crashed to ~USD 1.2 bn (about 2 weeks of imports). The Chandra Shekhar government (May 1991) pledged 47 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England; the subsequent Rao-Manmohan Singh government (July 1991) pledged another 20 tonnes to the Bank of Japan — raising ~USD 600 mn to avert default. The crisis triggered the 1991 economic reforms (LPG — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation). The IMF ALSO provided a Stand-By Arrangement but the short-term gold-pledge was the immediate rescue. World Bank and ADB gave longer-term project finance but weren't the emergency bridge. This episode is a GA staple — memorise 1991, gold, and 'LPG reforms'.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the CORRECT definition of 'BoP SURPLUS' under a floating exchange-rate regime like India's?

options.option_text: An ACCOUNTING impossibility — BoP always balances to zero by construction
The situation where total autonomous transactions produce a net inflow, leading to RESERVE ACCUMULATION by the central bank
The situation where the government runs a fiscal surplus
The situation where exports exactly equal imports

questions.explanation: Conceptually the BoP is split into AUTONOMOUS (voluntary, profit-motivated) transactions and ACCOMMODATING (balancing, via official reserves) transactions. A 'BoP surplus' is informally the excess of autonomous inflows over outflows — which the central bank accommodates by buying forex and INCREASING reserves. Technically, when reserves are included, the BoP sums to zero (accounting identity). Option A confuses the identity with economic meaning. Option C conflates fiscal policy with BoP. Option D describes balanced trade, not BoP surplus (services, transfers, capital flows all matter too).

questions.stem: Which of the following Indian authorities PUBLISHES the quarterly Balance of Payments data and the annual India's External Debt Status Report?

options.option_text: Ministry of Finance only
Reserve Bank of India (BoP data) and Ministry of Finance
Ministry of Commerce and NITI Aayog
SEBI and IRDAI

questions.explanation: RBI publishes BoP data QUARTERLY in its Development in India's BoP release. India's External Debt Status Report is published QUARTERLY jointly by the Ministry of Finance (Economic Affairs Dept.) and RBI — the latter maintains the external-debt database. These releases are public, freely downloadable, and are the canonical source for all macro analysis of India's external accounts. Option A undersells RBI's role. Options C and D describe authorities with no direct role in BoP accounting. External Debt Report jointly with RBI.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a determinant typically used to assess if a country's Current Account Deficit is 'SUSTAINABLE'?

options.option_text: CAD as % of GDP (commonly safe threshold < 3 %)
Composition of deficit financing (FDI preferred over 'hot money' FPI)
Stock of forex reserves (months of imports covered)
The domestic unemployment rate among PhD holders

questions.explanation: The three canonical sustainability tests for CAD: (i) CAD as % of GDP — below 3 % is considered manageable in emerging markets; (ii) QUALITY of financing — stable FDI (long-term, equity) better than FPI (short-term, 'hot money' that can reverse suddenly); (iii) Forex reserve adequacy — reserves covering 6-9 months of imports provide a cushion. Unemployment of PhDs (option D) has NO direct BoP-sustainability linkage — pure distractor. India's CAD was 1.2 % of GDP in FY24, financed largely by stable FDI + remittances — currently comfortable.
